questions.prompt: You see a wall of error text, most of it stack frames. What do you read first?
options: The middle frames, where the failure is
The first and last lines — one states the problem, the other usually suggests the next step
The top of the file the code lives in
questions.explanation: The first line says what went wrong and the last usually says what to do, so those two carry the most signal. Option A is tempting because the frames look dense and technical, but the middle is mostly context. Option C is about your last attempt, not this failure. Option D opens a file the error has not pointed you at yet.

questions.prompt: Claude Code suggested a fix. It did not work. What does that tell you?
options: Check whether the suggestion actually matched the error's first and last lines; if it did not, it was a guess
You need to restart the session
questions.explanation: A failed suggestion is a report about whether the fix was grounded in the error text — if it does not match the first and last lines, it was a guess. Option A is the tempting "tool is broken" move the reframe targets. Option C blames the error instead of checking the fix against it. Option D addresses nothing.

questions.prompt: An error reads `at Object.<anonymous> (/app/src/user.js:42:17)`. What is your next move?
options: Search the whole repo for the string `foo`
Open `/app/src/user.js` at line 42 and read the lines around it
Rerun the command a few times to see if it clears
Ignore the line number — it is usually wrong
questions.explanation: Most errors are local, so the file-and-line in the message is where to look and the surrounding lines give the context. Option A searches broadly for a name the error already narrowed down. Option C hopes a real failure is flaky. Option D discards the most specific clue the error gave you.

questions.prompt: An error from a tool call makes no sense to you. What is the best move?
options: Retype the error from memory into a search engine
Paste or quote the actual error text and ask Claude Code what it tells you
Guess a fix and try it
questions.explanation: The error is data — hand the real text to the tool, which is good at restating it in plainer words and pointing at the line. Option A is tempting, but a retyped error drifts and loses the detail that mattered. Option C is the guessing loop the lesson exists to cut. Option D throws away the context you need to understand the failure.
